extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of physiology, natural philosophy, and evolutionary theory (mid-19th century style)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts general physiological principles about how organisms develop organization: the roles of differentiation and integration, the tendency of homogeneous aggregates to become heterogeneous, and what structural apparatuses are a priori prescribable from physical/chemical conditions. Emphasizes deductive reasoning from basic facts to biological necessities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiations accompanied by integrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous is carried on by differentiations and accompanying integrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fusion of ganglia in adult crabs; differentiation of alimentary canal into stomach and intestine; replacement of many rudimentary hearts by a single heart in higher Annulosa; coalescence of vertebral processes with vertebral bodies. The changes in which several things become one (integration) demand recognition equally with those in which one thing becomes several (differentiation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration depends on community of function
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrations are in some way dependent on community of function: parts performing similar duties tend to unify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the eight segments coalescing to form a centipede's head jointly protect the cephalic ganglion and support jaws; bones uniting to form a vertebrate skull; pelvic consolidation and sacral ankylosis transferring body weight to legs; fusion of tibia/fibula and radius/ulna in ungulates reflecting limited limb rotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration is constrained by antagonistic functional requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendencies to integration are limited by other functional necessities, so integration may remain incomplete where further unification would impair other functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and counterexamples: the two eyes do not fully coalesce because binocular vision benefits from slightly different fields and because bringing orbits closer would reduce olfactory chambers; the nasal septum remains because it serves evaporating and nerve-supporting functions. These show integration can be antagonized by other tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher organisms are more differentiated from their medium
rubrics_metrics.description: On passing from lower to higher forms we pass to organisms more completely differentiated from the surrounding medium in multiple respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspects enumerated: structure (heterogeneity vs homogeneity), definiteness of form and size, chemical composition (higher organisms contain more organic elements and are chemically less like their medium), specific gravity contrasts, temperature (higher organisms maintain temperatures more distinct from environment), and self-mobility (greater locomotion contrasts with inert environment). Numerous examples compare protozoa, sponges, zoophytes, invertebrates, fishes, mammals, and birds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater contrast with environment correlates with superior vital manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which an organism differs from its inanimate medium (physically and chemically) is connected with its powers of activity and vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: organisms physically like their environment tend to be passive and affected by environmental changes; organisms more unlike their environment can actively compensate for changes. Examples contrast gelatinous low forms with active mammals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of deductive (a priori) reasoning from fundamental data
rubrics_metrics.description: Given certain fundamental physical and chemical conditions for vital activity, one may deduce a priori the necessity of certain structural apparatuses in organisms of given sizes and activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that, beyond inductive generalizations, physiologists can and do implicitly use deductions: from oxidation requirements deduce need for respiratory surfaces; from nutritive conditions deduce need for digestive cavities; from size/activity deduce need for vascular systems. The legitimacy of such deductions is supported by practical recognition among physiologists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a respiratory apparatus for bulky active organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: If an organism is bulky and exhibits considerable vital activity, mere integumental contact with oxygen is insufficient, and an extensive ramified respiratory surface (lungs, gills, branchiae, or equivalents) is predicable a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: oxygen for oxidation resides in the surrounding medium; small organisms may obtain it by surface contact, but larger/active ones require increased surface area for aeration (internal or external) — hence lungs or gills are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a digestive cavity for animals not constantly bathed in nutritive fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: Animals inhabiting media that are not in themselves nutritive must have appliances (a digestive cavity) to macerate, dissolve, and provide extended surfaces for absorption of food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast given: endoparasitic entozoa lack stomachs because bathed in nutritive fluid; other animals require a stomach/digestive cavity to perform solvent/macerating action and absorb dissolved products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a vascular (circulatory) system for large active organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Where bulk, activity, or both create need for widespread distribution of nutriment and oxygen, a system of blood-vessels or equivalent channels of conveyance is a priori inferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: simple branched canals in Medusae imply comparative inactivity; large, vivacious creatures must have a pulsating vascular system to supply concentrated nutriment and oxygen to every organ. The absence of conveyance channels limits usefulness of absorbed elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneity is an unstable equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: A homogeneous state is one of unstable equilibrium such that the slightest disturbance will destroy the arrangement and produce heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical and physical examples: a stick poised on its lower end, scales that cannot remain perfectly balanced, particles on a liquid concentrating into groups, a uniformly hot body cooling unevenly, and metal surfaces oxidizing. Social examples: equal properties/powers in a community quickly slide into inequalities. Instability is general and inevitable given differing external influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instability arises because parts are differently exposed to forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The instability of homogeneous aggregates follows from the fact that their several parts are necessarily exposed to different forces (in kind or amount) and thus become differently modified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: outside/inside relations and proximity to sources of influence mean parts receive unlike influences, producing unequal changes and loss of equilibrium; this explains both inductively and deductively why homogeneity cannot be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneous germs tend toward either decomposition or organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Homogeneous organic germs have a peculiar proclivity towards a non-homogeneous state, which may be either chaotic decomposition or orderly organization, depending on the modifying forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the feeble affinities of organic molecules and their sensitivity to heat, light, electricity, and chemical actions, a homogeneous aggregate of such molecules will gravitate towards heterogeneity. Whether the outcome is disorderly (decomposition) or orderly (organization) depends on the nature and intensity of the disturbing forces and whether organic compounds are preserved or destroyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental principle of organization: position-dependent differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: The many like units forming a germ acquire those kinds and degrees of unlikeness which their respective positions entail; organization arises because parts differently placed are differently modified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: outer parts vs inner parts, proximity to nutritive sources, exposure to light/heat/oxygen or maternal tissues — these positional relations determine the first differentiations leading to incipient organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of permanent positional relations prevents established differentiation (Amoeba exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creatures like Amoeba, which exhibit perpetual and irregular changes of shape and interchange of inner and outer parts, do not show persistent differentiations, because there are no settled positional relations for parts to be differently modified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: in Rhizopods the continual interchange of places means what was interior can become an external pseudopod and vice versa; without fixed relations of inner/outer, the positional mechanism for stable differentiation is absent, so no permanent organization develops.
